title: Kubernetes Solutions for Agent-Shaped Problems
tldr: Tim Hockin and Dmitry Berkovich explain why the obvious pod-per-agent-session pattern on Kubernetes gives slow starts and poor utilization, and how Agent Substrate fixes it with secure-by-default sandboxes, near-zero cost for idle agents and fast wake from layered snapshots. The long Q&A covers the policy enforcement point, snapshot invalidation and missing pieces such as autoscaling and automatic suspend.

key_points.text: Agent workloads are bursty (work for 100 ms to half a minute, then idle for hours), run untrusted generated code that needs full isolation, and have a human waiting for responses.
Pod per session wastes requested resources while the user thinks, then destroys the pod on timeout and pays the slow sandbox start again on return.
Teams that rolled their own ran many sandboxes inside large pods, then needed a control plane across nodes, effectively rebuilding Kubernetes.
Three principles: security (no network by default, everything sandboxed, per-agent identity), density (idle agents cost about zero) and speed (wake feels like it never slept).
Built on Kubernetes: workers are pods, the control plane and policy run in the cluster, and on node drain workers move their agents elsewhere.
Concepts: actor (one session), actor template, worker (a pod hosting many actors), outlet (per-node manager handling images and snapshots), and ATE net with a router and an egress.
Actors have no IP; the router finds the actor from the DNS name, holds the request while it resumes the actor, and the egress applies policy and injects credentials.

Snapshots have layers: OCI image, a mandatory volume, root FS diffs and memory. Same image and machine type allows a full resume; a new image throws away memory and root FS for a cold start from the volume.
Common pattern: a managed agent loop such as Gemini (brains) calls Substrate inside your own perimeter (hands), where work can be audited and stopped.
The policy enforcement point is a plug-in: actor traffic is wrapped in HTTP CONNECT and sent to it; Envoy and Solo.io's agentgateway are the two implementations so far.
Suspend writes a local snapshot, then uploads it asynchronously; the scheduler prefers a node that still holds the latest copy. Only the durable directory is guaranteed to persist.

numbers.text: Sandbox pod startups seen at 15 seconds, 30 seconds and up to a couple of minutes.
Aspirational goals: billions of agents in one cluster, 10,000+ activations per second, wake in about 100 ms.
In 1.0, snapshot upload to cloud storage starts after 5 minutes suspended.
Users have been in production since 0.2, released two months ago; the project has been built for about 6 months.

open_gaps.text: No good autoscaling story for worker pods and nodes; HPA on CPU and memory does not fit agents that sleep and wake often, so sizing is manual today.
Memory management is imperfect: no in-place resource updates, and a hostile workload can still exhaust memory.
Suspend is manual or harness-driven; detecting idleness automatically is unsolved, and self-suspend is coming.
Base image patches invalidate memory and root FS snapshots for every affected actor; merging overlays is an open question.

opportunities.text: Write a third policy enforcement point implementation for Substrate egress.
Design autoscaling signals for Substrate worker pools from activation and suspend activity rather than CPU.
Make your agent harness call suspend when a task finishes, and keep needed state in the durable directory.
The brains/hands split for running managed agent loops against compute inside your own security perimeter.
